note: Cohort selection criteria are part of the method, so they are versioned next to the rubric rather than buried in code. Matching is case-insensitive, on word boundaries, against TITLE + DESCRIPTION only. The server NAME is deliberately excluded: the registry's io.github.* convention puts the word 'github' in the name of every GitHub-hosted server, which made a name-inclusive filter match 6,075 of 6,999 npm servers. Excluding the name drops the pool to 299 with visibly higher precision.

dev-tooling.label: Developer tooling
dev-tooling.why_this_one_for_the_spike: Largest installable population in the registry, no credential requirement to enumerate tools, and no overlap with the CBRE conflict surface. The spike proves the instrument; the measurement, not taste, later names the vertical to commit to.
dev-tooling.include_note: Only terms that name the SUBJECT of a dev-tooling server. Weak terms that appear in boilerplate for every server ('code', 'api', 'cli', 'build', 'docs', 'python', 'rust', 'docker') were removed after they matched 87% of the npm population.
dev-tooling.known_false_positives: Terms like 'lsp', 'ci/cd' and 'coding agent' pull in a handful of adjacent servers (game engines, observability suites, prompt tools). match_terms is recorded per selected server so any false positive is visible in the cohort file rather than hidden in a count.

ranking.rationale: Ranking by real installs biases the cohort toward servers a buyer might actually have installed, which is the population an audit is sold against. The download figure is pinned into the cohort file so the selection is auditable after the fact.
ranking.known_bias: Download counts favour older and vendor-published servers. This is a spike cohort, not a random sample of the registry, and must not be described as one.
